name: CS1101S: Programming Methodology
intro: The first module that CS students take in NUS, CS1101S is a module that introduces students to the world of programming through a gamified platform.
breakdown: 18%: Source Academy Achievements: 0.75% per level up to Level 24
review: CS1101S was my first proper run in with programming, not counting the self learning I did with Harvard CS50. With little to no prior knowledge in programming, I was expecting to struggle quite a bit and oh boy did I struggle. The whole course was conducted in the gamified platform of Source Academy, with weekly assignments in the form of missions and quests. While I do appreciate the fact that they are trying to appeal to us with the idea of games, it personally ended up being a lot more of a hindrance in my learning. Imagine hearing about recursion for the first time and the next moment, you are presented with a bunch of runes and asked to make fractals for some mission. Like, what? I would have preferred a more traditional approach instead of all the fanstasy fluff context. It also was weird that they restricted us to using Source, a restricted version of Javascript. I understand that they wanted to instill the very basic concepts of programaming in us instead of blindly spamming loops everywhere, but I am pretty sure there are better ways to go about doing this. I felt like there were alot of redundant concepts too, some of which should definitely not be in the introduction course for Y1 students: meta-circular evaluator??, whatever that sound and graphic assignment was, and the unnecessarily complex functional expressionism mission. Assessments like the Reading Assessments were tricky but doable. Practical Assessment is basically Leetcode with kinda insane time crunch. Midterms and Finals felt like RNG for me, but I am sure people who have solid foundation found it a breeze. Might be a hot take, but I did enjoy the assessment breakdown, especially for a module like this. It was nice to have multiple chances to prove understanding of the content throughout the entire semester instead of a single final exam, rewarding people who take a consistent studying approac instead of the classic last minute revision style. Though I didn't personally approach any teaching staff outside of the studio sessions with Owen and Eldric (TAs for studio and recitation), I did hear/see that the teaching staff were generally very approacable and helpful, so props to them.
closingRemarks: I do have many thoughts on how to improve the module, whether it be the content being taught or the way it is delivered. However, there must be a reason why it is still done the way it is for so long. Maybe I am the fussy one 😨. Honestly though, it is a passable module, definitely not the worst but not necessarily the best too.

name: CS1231S: Discrete Mathematics
intro: Rather infamous module that covers discrete mathematics. People call it an S/U module, blaming its difficulty and the fact that it covers really dry content
review: Felt kind of apprehensive going into this module, assuming that there was going to be a lot of mathematical concepts and proofs to be done. And I was somewhat right. The module covers quite a significant amount of content, especially in the second half in my opinion. The first half introduces you to some familiar concepts of mathematical notation and logical operations. This is where methods of proofs were shown and set theory was covered as well. Going into midterms, while I was not particularly confident, I still felt that the module was actually manageable and somewhat enjoyable to a degree. The second half was where things got more challenging, with the introduction of more complex concepts: Relation, Functions, Cardinality, Counting, Graphs and Trees. Oh boy, those were not as easy to understand. I assume this is the part that caused many of my seniors and peers to lament this module and  proceed to give up on this module and I can see why. Content was definitely drier and more abstract with proofs becoming more complex and seemingly undoable for a plebian like me. Funnily enough, I felt better going into finals than midterms and surprisingly did not do as well. I guess the content was indeed too much for me to handle. That said, I must say the workload is not too heavy. Other than lectures, tutorials and 2 assignments across the whole semester, there is no other forms of workload. The time consuming part is probably just trying to make sense of whatever was covered during the lectures because there is no way anyone can take in everything from the lecture in one go. Prof Aaron is a great lecturer and honestly helped lectures be more bearable. Prof Leong is also knowledgable assuming you can make it past the first 10 minutes where his voice somehow is always really raspy and hard to hear. My tutorial was taken by a Y4 student who seemed really dedicated and willing to do extra to prepare for his tutorials. Overall, teachign staff was pretty good and helpful.
closingRemarks: Overall, pretty decent module. It is definitely challenging but is not as unbearable as people make it out to be. Even though I did not necessarily do really well for the module, I still enjoyed the process. If only I was more mathematically inclined, I would have probably enjoyed it more and feel more accomplished going through the module.

name: EL1101E: The Nature of Language
intro: A fun module I chanced upon while looking for a module to clear my Cross-Disciplinary requirement. I have always been interested in gathering gathering somewhat niche knowledge and this seemed like a good fit.
review: Introductory module on linguistics, particularly focusing on the English language. The module covers a wide range of topics, from phonetics to morphology to syntax to semantics. The content is interesting and engaging, with the lecturer, Dr Leslie, being very passionate about the subject. The lectures are interactive and engaging, with Leslie often asking questions and encouraging students to participate. I had the opportunity to have him as my tutor as well for tutorial sessions. He was a very easygoing and is charismatic enough to keep me interested the whole time. The problem sets were a good way to reinforce your understanding of the material, and the tutorial participation component encourages you to engage with your peers and share your ideas, especially since there are no official solutions; instead the collective agreed intepretation derived from class discussion is taken to be the 'answer'. Understandable I guess, since language and linguistics are subjective in nature. The class test was completely open book but of course, the paper was set such that Google will not be much help as well. The individual essay was an interesting assignment where we had to write an essay covering 2 or more topics covered during the course. It had been a really long time since I've written anything but honestly, it was a nice break from the technical and mathy assignments I've been doing -- I ended up writing about the language used in a gaming and streaming context. The weekly workload was not too heavy as well, just the problem set attempts and some readings meant as lecture preparation.
closingRemarks: Fun and chill module, perfect for people who are looking for a break from the usual technical modules. The content is interesting and the workload is not too heavy.

name: GESS1029: Everyday Ethics in Singapore
intro: Another chill module I found in order to fulfill one of the GE pillars. I have always had many thoughts on various controversial topics surrounding Singapore, so what better module to take than one that would be cover them from an academic standpoint
review: Rather insightful module that sheds a lot of light on many issues that plague Singapore. Topics covered included: Inequality, Meritocracy, Multicultaralism and Migration, all of which are very relevant to Singapore. I did not attend lectures physically but from the recordings, I could tell they were done well by the lecturer, Daryl Ooi. He was able to engage the students well while getting his points acroos and also had provided multiple opportunities for students to discuss among themselves and share their own views on vaiorus points raised. The weekly readings could potentially be heavy, depending on how fast a reader you are, and yopur ability to understand the content, but personally I found it manageable. Reading quizzes only had 5 questions each, but were quite tricky at times, so making sure to reference the articles again were important. Having a friend to do the quizzes together is definitely a good idea. I particularly enjoyed the journal entries, where we had to reflect and just share our thoughts on the specific topic covered. It was an interesting assignment that really allowed me to explore my own thoughts on a specific topic without having to worry about writing ability or correctness. The group report and presentation were a bit of a hassle, for someone like me who really REALLY doesn't like interaction with others. Fortunately, it was not demanding at all and I was lucky enough to have an extroverted groupmate who carried with a lot of the talking aspects. As for finals, I found it quite similar to the reading quizzes, with both free giveaway questions as well as tricky ones. It was the first time, I saw so many students leave the exam hall early but being the paranoid person I am, I stayed till the end even though I was also done midway through the 2 hours. Overall, this module gave me a chance to bounce off the ideas and perspectives presented by not only the teaching staff, but also the peers around me to further refine my own personal opinions and the way I view Singapore society as a whole.
closingRemarks: People hype up GES1035 as the goto S/U module for clearing the SS pillar, but honestly I would recommend this as well, not as an S/U module but as a very light workload module that is also very insightful and somewhat easy to do well in with minimum effort.

name: MA2001: Linear Algebra I
review: First math module I had the pleasure of taking in NUS. I wouldn't say I am naturally talented at Math but I would not say I disliked it either. However, this was the start of a very deep hatred for anything mathematical. The module covers the basics of linear algebra, starting with linear systems and matrices, then moving on to more complex topics like euclidean spaces, vector sapces, orthogonality and transformations. I wouldn't say that the content was too difficult to understand, but it was just super dry. The way the lectures were done were also not to my liking. Having to watch several videsos of pre-lecture content followed by the actual 2hr sessions of rambling in hard to understand accents was just not it for me. The weekly quizzes were also a real pain to do and many defaulted to just using Wolfram|Alpha online or just begging for answers in the Telegram chat. Having to suddenly get used to proving problems requiring a solid understanding of the content was also a real pain. If you didn't have a friend group or at least one other to collab Homeworks with, good luck to you. For the big 60% Finals, I am pretty sure not many people completed it. The first few question parts were giveaway but the last 2 big questions were there solely to differentiate the students and help the bell curve and seemed completely impossible to do for the average person. I did like my TA Luka though. Guy was quite chill and efficient in his tutorials and was always willing to help out. Just a sidenote, the classroom was a real pain to get to. Having to take a lift from the back entrance of the building and enter through the back door is something a fresh Y1 student would not think to do. I ended up missing the bulk of the first tutorial simply because I, and a few others were locked out of the building because we took the lift from the front entrance which seemed like the obvious thing to do.
closingRemarks: As someone who really didn't enjoy vectors in JC, this was not an enjoyable module. Looking back now, it definitely is very useful though and I lowkey regret not putting more effort here. Still, given a chance, I won't do it again lol.

name: CS2040S: Data Structures and Algorithms
intro: Arguably the most important module in the CS curriculum, DSA is the backbone of everything CS no matter what area you wish to pursue.
review: First off, this was the first module I took where the grade breakdown was not given at all and honestly I felt that that was a very based decision from Prof Seth. He constantly reiterated that the module was not at all about grades and that the main goal is to learn and understand the content well. Honestly felt refreshing to see him get a little pissed at the unbearable CS zoom chat which kept asking about grade breakdown after he already covered his stance on it multiple times. He is a really good teacher but was let down by the fact that there is simply way too much content to cover in the 13 weeks. On top of having to learn Java on the fly, we covered basically every single data structure and algorithm you can think of, from linked lists to trees to graphs to sorting algorithms to hashing and even dynamic programming. Ince again, I wouldn't say the workload was very heavy, it just required consistent viewing of the lectures, attending tutorials and the somewhat weekly coding assignments on Coursemology. Tutorials or at least mine in particular were not the most helpful, since my TA did not seem like the most familiar with teaching given that he literally took the module a semester before, but he still gave it his best and I don't blame him for it. The assignments could range from simple to hard but with the help of my good friend Github, it was not too hard to complete them, albeit at the cost of my own understanding and learning. Coursemology XP was not too hard to accumulate especially with the lecture quizzes and tutorial attendance but Midterm and Finals was a whole different ballgame. It was all MCQ/MRQ but honestly at this point I would rather have open ended questions and proving questions back because I could at least get some (I hope) partial marks from those. These MCQ/MRQ questions were basically full on gambling for me because 1. The problem statement was too long and complex to understand, 2. The unnecessary large amopunt of options they gave were way too long, complex and similar to one another, 3. Required a lot of time to process even with a solid foundation of the content, or 4. ALL OF THE ABOVE. I was very sure I would do badly for the finals and even I did not expect myself to end up as the 10% percentile. Miraculously stil managed to scrape a B grade but it was a tough module, assessment wise for sure.
closingRemarks: Enjoyable Prof; Not so enjoyable content. Pretty sure some of the content covered could be pushed over the other modules, which would make it so much more manageable and also make sense teaching wise, but I am but a lowly student with no say in such issues.

name: CS2100: Computer Organization
intro: The supposed 'driest' of the holy trinity of CS modules, CS2100 is a module that covers the basics of computer organisation and architecture.
review: The supposed follow up to CS1231S, though without the need to do proofs anymore (thank god). The module covers the basics of computer organisation and architecture, starting from the very basics of binary and hexadecimal, before moving on to C and MIPS assembly language, the inner workings of a processor (honing in and control and datapath), everything about circuits and roundign up with caching and pipelining. Once again, the content covered was definitely the reason as to why people do not like this module, and I would have to agree. The prep work required to understand the lectures was quite a lot. In the first half, we had to learn a new counting system as well as the C programming language as they were prerequisites for what comes after, assembly language, in this case MIPS. MIPS really was pretty time consuming to make sense of and even after, it still required a lot of effort to understand it and be able to translate C to MIPS and vice versa. The scary part was that, if I remembered correctly, the beginning portion was simply so that we could go on to understand the actual content of the module, namely the subsequent topics on the processor, how circuits worked and pipelining and caching. These topics added a whole new layer of difficulty and complexity to this module and it really sucked for those that were not able to keep up with the earlier half. Nonetheless, contrary to most people's opinion, I actually quite enjoyed the module. I really vibed with Prof Colin's lecture style, something about it just made me want to listen to the lectures and learn. The assignments were not impossibly hard but also pose enough of a challenge for you to have to think abit and not just cruise through them. Labs were a bit of a hassle, especially the since physical attendance is required and the only slot I could get was at 9am on Mondays. Having to wake up at 7am every week just for a 1hr session that usually ends in 20minutes was not a good experience. Difficulty wise, the labs were definitely manageable and I particularly enjoyed the hands on we had with implementing circuits on the lab circuit board. Midterm was surprislingly manageable for the most part and likewise Finals was too. The former was more of a time scramble while the latter involved more thinking and calculation espcially with the caching and pipeling questions. I ended up not doing as well as I expected but I was satisfied with the knowledge I gained from the module.
closingRemarks: Quite a fun module despite its difficulty. I probably lucked out with the Finals being easier given the fact that it was open book but I'll take it.

name: ES2660: Communicating in the Information Age
intro: The first of 2 dreaded 'presentation' modules that all CS students have to face. Most people take it early on with the intention to S/U this module and I went in with the same mindset.
breakdown: 35%: CA1 - SOP for online information consumption (Individual critical response + group presentation)
review: I honestly don't really know what to talk about this module. As much as I really hated anything to do with public speaking and presentations, i can't really blame them for adding this to our core curriculum. Content wise, it covered 2 different critical thinking frameworks which ended up as the basis for CA1. I was fortunate enough to take the same tutorial class with a few others I knew/got to know and we were able to get through the group work portion relatively well. As for CA2, it comprised writing a commentary on a specific focal text of our own choice that adheres to the umbrella theme of 'Engineering Trust in Digital Transformation'. Most people did not like this but this portion was the easier for me since its basically just an individual essay about your own opinion. nothing to hard to come up with. Getting used to formal writing was a pain but it ended up fine. CA3 was the impromptu speaking portion, where we had to present a speech on a random topic given to us 5 minutes before the presentation. I was not confident at all in my speaking abilities and I was right to be so. We did have many practise sessions before but even then I did not volunteer to speak at all. For the actual assessment, I ended up getting a topic on a specific book and I ended up being able to smoke out some speech that seemed coherent enough to me but it still did not feel great leading up to it. The feeling after however was heavenly, knowing that I was done with this module. Class participation consisted of attendance, the classic raising and answering questions as well as facilitating discussion and lastly a panel discussion that everyone has to take part in. Personally, I think I prepared sufficiently for the discussion but I kind of got 'sabotaged' by another classmate who was being immature and intentionally difficult with accepting responses. Also had the pleasure of getting a difficult question straight from the tutor because no one else was asking questions after my elaboration (maybe I was that thorough with my research, definitely not coping). All in al, it really felt like a big weight off my chest when I was done with this module. It contained a lot of fluff content but taking it with others definitely made it more bearable. Props to Jodie, the tutor and also the module coordinator, she really tried her best to make the module as engaging as possible.
closingRemarks: Would not do ever again. No matter how much I try to sugarcoat it, I just can't. No flame to the teaching staff, but these kinds of communication modules are just not for me.

name: GEA1000: Quantitative Reasoning with Data
intro: Yet another module that most NUS students take to clear the data literacy pillar.
review: I don't have much to say about this module to be really honest. It went just as I had imagined after reading the description and objectives of the course. The lectures were in the form of short videos meant for us to watch at our own pace. Tutorials were every other week, meaning workload was considerably low compared to other modules a freshman would take. Content wise, it also wasn't difficult at all, it covers very elementary statistic concepts like the 5 number summary and also taught us how to use Excel and R to do some basic data analysis. Quizzes were not hard and tutorial sessions, while long, were okay for the most part. For the group presentation, each group was given an article and then do analysis and present our findings and conclusion to the tutor in the last week. I was fortunate enough to have a group willing to commit to the module, contrary to some others who went in with the intention to S/U it. Group presentation went well and I honestly didn't feel to nervous this time since it was just presenting to one person, our tutor and there were no restrictions on reading off a script. Finals however, took me by surprise. It was not the hardest per se but I definitely underestimated it and did not prepare well enough. I ended up making many careless mistakes which ultimately costed me quite a lot given the steep bell curve. Overall, a decent module both in terms of difficulty, workload and potential to score well.
closingRemarks: Very touch and go elementary statistics module meant for all university students regardless of major. If you are looking to just clear the GE pillar, this is fine, else you can opt for the alternatives like DSA1101 and ST1311.

name: GEC1009: Drugs and Society
intro: As the name suggests, this module covers the topic of drugs and its impact on society. Nothing really much more to it.
review: I went into this module wiht the intention of satisfying some of my curiosity about knowledge on drugs, specifically the scientific aspect of them; how they are made, how they work and what they do. Initially, there was a glimpse of that, but as expected from the module title, it quickly became more of a history lesson  instead, covering the hisroty of drug use in the past on how it shapes society now in the present. Content got stale pretty quickly and I found myself not as interested in the module as I was when bidding for it in the first place. After sharing with a friend in Pharmacy, I also got to know that one of the lecturers + module coordinator also did not really have a good reputation. All in all, content-wise started out mildy interesting but petered out somewhat quickly into the semester. That is on me though, since I should have expected that given the module title and description. The real problem with this module is the workload. Keep in mind that this is merely a GE module at Level-1000. The fact that this module had comparable workload to some Level-2000 CS modules I was taking that semester 2 was not a good sign. CA1 and Finals are dismissable since they were one off assessments, but the addition of 3 separate CA assignments seemed excessive to me. Additionally, they weren't the kind of tasks where you could simply complete easily. One of them was a group project report + presentation that obviously will not go well for a module where you don't even get to meet your randomly assignmed groupmates. The other 2 were individual assignments with a creative twist  -- a graphic commentary and a video blog, making grading becoming increasingly subjective. I wanted to take this module to counteract stress from CS modules but it ended up being a source of stress itself, with the CS modules actually helping me relax more. ??? The best part is they announced mid-semester that this module was phasing out at the end of the semester, so I was basically the last batch to take this module at Level-1000, because the workload was indeed recognised to be way higher than reflected and it was being revamped into a Level-2000 module. Just my luck to have to sit through this module.
closingRemarks: TLDR: S/U module especially if you are taking this to fill up space in your timetable. Workload is significantly heavier than other level-1000 modules especially a GE module.

name: MA1521: Calculus for Computing
intro: The other foundational math module that CS students have to take, MA1521 covers calculus.
review: One look at the assessment breakdown and you already know you won't be scoring well unless you are a Math major, willing to put in a whole lot of effort or simply Math prodigy. Content wise, it started building on JC calculus before covering more advanced topics like multivariable, indefinete calculus, polar coordinates etc. The main issue was pacing. They essentially spedrun about 4 years worth of calculus content into a few weeks, assuming you are still fresh from JC (RIP my fellow NSmen), before moving straight into the more advanced and new concepts. Lectures were not worth it at all, with the lecturer just following through the slides and boring the whole audience. I didn't attend a single tutorial at all because the tutorial questions were manageable enough and honestly didn't seem to warrant extra help. BUT, the online quizzes were a different story. Those questions spike in difficulty and honestly sucks because each individual question is 1% of your full grade given the weightage. Finals was similar with the difficulty much higher than those found in tutorials, catching many people off guard if they were not able to get their hands on PYPs.
closingRemarks: Just do the bare minimum and try to cram a few days before the Final. Remember your cheatsheet, you will definitely need it. If you are satisfied with your minimum effort grade, good for you, else just S/U it and don't think about it anymore. Not worth giving more effort than necessary.

name: CFG1003: Financial Wellbeing Introduction
intro: Simple OTOT e-learning module
review: Pretty sure most people take this because it is required to take CFG1004, a popular 2 mc module. Pretty much covers simple financial concepts to do with budgeting and managing your money. Its mostly common sense and should not take more than half a day to complete, should you wish to thoroughly read through the interactive slides .
closingRemarks: No harm taking this module, especially if you are planning to take CFG1004.

name: CS2030S: Programming Methodology II
intro: A follow up to the first CS module, CS2030S covers more advanced programming concepts and paradigms in the Java language.
review: The last of the holy trinity of CS modules, CS2030S covers topics like OOP, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, abstract classes, generics, exceptions, streams, lambdas, and more. The workload was not too heavy, prior to previous semester because the supposed killer weekly labs were modified and made simpler for some reason. There were also no tutorials and the weekly recitations merely served as an recap of the week's content and some form of reinforcement learning. Nonetheless, it was still somewhat of a time sink since the labs were tedious having to do it in VIM, which honestly is not great despite what some people say. The assessments (Midterm and Final) honestly can range in difficulty depending on topics you focus on while revising but should generally include some free marks and some subparts that you could hazard a guess and aim some partial credit. Personally, the real headache for me were the two timed Practical Assessments. Having to refer to a problem statement and refactor and/or write new code that adheres to certain requirements was not easy, especially when you have to do it in a limited time frame. It was good having a small bit of Java experience given I took CS2040S the semester before, though that only lasted a week or 2. While CS2040S did use Java, it only covered very very basic syntax whereas CS2030S focused a lot more on the correctness of code and taught us how to write good and sensible code while abiding by various principles. I must say this module was quite enjoyable despite content being slightly heavy, dry and complex at times. Prof Adi is a great lecturer and I appreciated his cheery nature and humour. The way he explains concepts is also concise and he doesn't hesitate to help students in clarifying concepts be it during lecture, recitations or honestly anytime. Furthermore, as the only professor coordinating such a big module, it is testament to his ability and dedication to the module. Other modules should definitely learn from him. I also appreciate the fact that he is a fellow otaku and often sets papers with questions revolving around certain games or anime he currently has interest in (I had a One Piece themed paper and I heard they recently had a Tears of the Kingdom and a Jujutsu Kaisen themed paper). Setting aside the glazing for now, CS2030S definitely gave me insight into the world of programming, allowing me to understand that there is a lot more to writing code than just writing efficient code catered to certain problems as seen in CS2040S. All in all, the workload does not seem too heavy, but the content is definitely more complex and requires more time to understand and digest, especially in the second half. However, should you be able to break down everything taught and internalise it, you should be able to score well in this module and most definitely feel very accomplished.
closingRemarks: You have to take this as a CS student no matter what, so honestly just try your best to go in with a positive mindset. I feel that this is the first module that actually teaches you how to code better, which I felt should have been covered in its prerequisite, CS1101S.

name: CS2105: Introduction to Computer Networks
intro: First non core CS module I took, and one that would contribute to a Networks Focus Area I planned on pursuing.
review: Frankly, the main incentive to taking this module was that it is part of the Networks Focus Area which seemed to be the easiest focus area to achieve while having the least workload compared to other ones such as god forbid, Algorithms or Artificial Intelligence. However, I was quite enjoying the content in the first half of the module. It seemed like more of a trivia module with concepts not being fully delved into, given the fact it is an intro module but it covered enough to keep me interested. Second half, I started to lose interest due to the way the lecture was conducted which felt a lot more seminar-style, with the professor sharing a lot of his own experiences and stories and expecting discussion with his audience. I can't really explain it but I did not vibe as well with this style and ended up not even watching the recorded lectures and merely relied on the slides and Google to learn the second half content. Workload as promised was relatively light, with tutorials literally taking 20 minutes to complete max each week. The 3 lab assignments were also not too difficult with the help of Github. Midterms was a relatively manageable MCQ paper with difficulty only attributed to some trickiness and the most random and obscure fact you could find in the slides that was barely covered but still examinable (RFC???). Finals gave us open ended questions which was a nice change until you realise that they completely reused an old paper, which meant that students who managed to get the paper and print it out for this OPEN BOOK exam were basically guaranteed full marks. The teaching staff were also very reluctant to giving out PYPs possibly due to this but of course, some students found a way to get it anyway. Still, I did fairly well and was somewhat entertained in the first half, so I would say it is a decent module.
closingRemarks: Potentially easiest non core CS intro module you can take. If you are looking for a chill module to take, this is it.

name: CS2109S: Introduction to AI and Machine Learning
intro: The newest addition into the core CS curriculum if I am not mistaken. Notorious reputation since its inception under Prof Ben Leong but I was willing to give it a shot earlier into University to get the pain over with quickly and boy it did pay off.
review: There are definitely many complaints about the module, but I feel that some of them are unjustified and mostly due to the bias against Prof Ben Leong, who I won't say I am a fan off but purely based on its content and assessment structure, I do feel the module is not as bad as people make it out to be. The module covers the very basics of AI and ML, with AI being the focus in the first half and ML in the latter half. Starting with the first half, I would say the introduction to AI and some technical jargon was fine. The refresher on sorting such as BFS and DFS was manageable too. We then moved on to newer searches such as A* and minimax with alpha beta pruning which took some effort to learn and understand but for the most part, it was doable. The main issue for me was heuristics and once again, proofs return to give me problems. I found it hard to prove why a certain heuristic works or exhibits certain attributes like admissability, consistency and dominance. This, alongside an unfotunate wrong intepretation of a problem definition essentially costed me my Midterms, which I did really really badly for (2 s.d. below mean lol). From then, I was basically giving up on this module and just wanted to get through it and scrape a pass. It helped that Coursemology XP was relatively easy to accumulate with the large amount of opportunities to gain them just by consistently attending tutorials, doing lecture quizzes and attempting the problem sets. The content in the second half was also not tested in a pen and paper final (more on that later), so I was comfortable simply treating the second half content as more of a trivia module and focusing on other modules instead. I had the opportunity to have the Head TA as my tutorial TA and she was good in conducting the classes, starting out with a recap of the past lecture's content before moving on with discussing the tutorial questions. Nothing really more to add there. As for the Problem Sets, for some reason, I struggled the most in the first PS0 which aimed to give us a crash course on python, matrices and NumPy, things we were going to encounter a lot further down in the module. Subsequent Psets got somewhat more manageable given the help of ChatGPT (haha use AI to solve AI) and collaboration with friends. As the content covered became more complex, so did the assistance provided in the Pset, since they really are trying to teach the concepts and they do not expect a newbie to be able to code something like a full CNN on their own. Now, we finally come to the star of the module, the Final assessment. If i remember correctly, the semester I took this module was its 4th iteration, and they had been trying different forms of assessments. In my semester, they stuck to the previous year's method of a take home timed coding/practical assessment, whereby we had a full 28 hours so deliver and submit a ML model that works well on the provided dataset, Grading would be done based on the accuracy of your submitted model, compared against the rest of the cohort. Additionally, there is also a report component which merely served as free marks, if you properly document information according to its requirements (basically guarantees you do not get a 0). Let's just say it was definitely a Finals to remember. I was really glad I attempted the Mock PA that they realised a week before the actual Finals because it gave me an idea of what to expect. My particular Final involved creating a model that could take image data as input and output a certain value. I ended up staying up a full 12 hours from the assignment release time to 8 am the next morning to create a decently working model before sleeping. I then spent that evening refining it more and making a few changes before submitting it with no issues. I was not too confident in my model but was decently satisfied with the effort I put in, aiming to hit at close to upper quartile based on the regular benchmark updates they provided. I was really surprised to find out I actually did really well for the Finals component, and it ending up compensating for tha abhorrent midterm I had. I ended up with a B+ grade, which was a huge relief for me. To summarise, content wise, I am not the best judge for it but I felt that the first half was definitely doable. The second half is when a lot of math is introduced and for some reason skimmed over. To add on, the fact that it was barely tested in the Finals essentially meant that many people did not pay much atention to it, so while it is alot more abstract and difficult I do not have much recollection on it. Workload wise, it is definitely on the heavier side, but it is manageable if you are able to keep up with the content and not fall behind. The Psets were meant to be completed in a day and should not pose much of a problem if work is done consistently. The moment there is backlog, thats when things get difficult, but that could be said for nay module out there to be honest. The Finals was definitely the highlight of the module, and I would say it was a good experience to have, especially since it was the first of its kind I have ever experienced. But maybe that's just in hindsight. I really would not want to do it again. The biggest issue of this module, however is the admin. The fact that our midterm results were only released in lat final week of the semester already tells you what you need to know. Mistakes in the lecture slides are admissible as that is human nature. Late release of Problem Sets or issues with them due to the TAs are also fine; we all make mistakes. But the fact that the midterm results release kept on getting postponed with no actual updates on its progress except, `we are still working on it`, is not acceptable. I rather a truthful statement like, `We have not enough manpower` or `I had other academic committments` than to be kept in the dark or worse given a vague statement. The way the submission of the Finals was also handled poorly in my opinion even though it did not concern me as much. The Finals was conducted on the weekend of recess week, with the submission dealine at 2359 of the day before the first day of Examination week. Several people who had morning exams the next day were not happy with this. Coupled with the fact that the load on the Coursemology servers the evening of submission was so high that many people had trouble checking and submitting their work, it was a recipe for disaster. I was not affected since I did my checks earlier and followed the advice to incremently submit my work guarantee a submission should there be any issues such as this but clearly, many didn't listen. To keep things short and from an objective viewpoint, I would say that the students having troubles with submitting and still venting, complaining and even cursing on the forum is just not acceptable. We are all adults here and that sort of childish behaviour is not warranted. Sure that sort of thing would definitely cause a lot of stress on those experiencing it, and indeed it is also partly the teaching staff's fault for not anticipating this even though they conducted the same assessment style the semester before and deemed it workable for this semester too, but to throw a tantrum on the forum just further makes me digusted to be a part of this CS cohort with those people. As much as I am not a fan of the administrative side of this module (honeslt just the midterm result fiasco), they should not be judged to harshly for the Finals incident. Sure, they may have underestimated tohe load on the servers but they did try to circumvent the issue by advising people to, as mentioned before, incremently submit your work and not submit in the last minute or in this case hour, but people just did not listen. Still, they did leave the submission dealine open for a few more hours into the night to allow those affected to submit their work, so I would say that they did try to rectify the issue as best they could. And for those that did complain about fairness of this decision, honestly just piss off.
closingRemarks: In summary, you can definitely tell that there is a lot more room for improvement in the module, but I would say it is not as bad as people make it out to be.

name: HSI1000: How Science Works, Why Science Works
intro: Basic CHS module that most FASS students take in their first year. No idea why I took it but I did.
review: Went in expecting a lot of fluffy content and I did get that, but there were also some interesting takeaways I got from it. There were 3 main blocks of content, each covered by about 4 weeks of lectures each, taken by a different Prof. Lectures were mostly fine, but honestly, I had other modules to worry about, and mainly used the recordings as background noise while doing other work; they were not really necessary and you could do without them but I have a habit of just 'watching' them anyway. The tutorials or workshops were long and more seminar like with a lot of class discussion and participation marks. Not exactly my favourite but I survived. My TA was also very chill and engaging to the experience was not to bad. The labs/exploratoriums were basically lower secondary or even primary school style science practical experiments. Pretty simple and you do it in groups with the only submission being a report of your findings at the end. A little RNG based on where you sit but most people get decent marks for it anyway. They aren't trying to fail you here. Come one, it's an intro CHS module. Midterm and Finals were both open book MCQ/MRQ papers. People struggled with the time aspect but I usually am good with that so I managed fine. Questions were mainly common sense and some were CTRL + F-able, so bell curve was rather steep. The highlight of the module was probably the assignment where the task was to visit a nature reserve and do a bunch of tasks there like measuring trees and observing the different species of flora and fauna. I went with a willing friend and honestly even though it ended up raining, it had been a long time since i went out an dactually physically touched grass, so it was a pleasant experience. The report took a lot more time to cook up than I expected but it was fine. Surprisingly, this module was one of the more enjoyable modules I took this semester, despite the fluffy content and social interaction requirement.
closingRemarks: Managed to clear the module for my Interdisciplinary requirement + they managed to get me out of my room and touch grass. Props to them.

name: IS1108: Digital Ethics and Data Privacy
intro: Fluffiest module in the world. Redundant module.
review: Don't want to spend too much time on this because it simply isn't worth my time. Pretty sure most people or at least the normal functioning people in society who have an ounce of common sense already know a thing or 2 about ethics. The fact that this module is even a thing is beyond me. How is somethign like ethics even gradeable. Its basically all common sense, but somehow the module was able to produce 12 weeks worth of content with lectures and even 2 to 3 videos on it per week. The tutorials were also a joke, with the tutors seeming like they don't really care too. This semester, they revamped their assessment system because of the many issues they faced the previous semester adn they added more CA componenents. Now, every tutorial essentially requires group discussion and presentation of a MIRO board analysing the ethics of a given problem statement from the perspective of various parties. the thing is, I don't think anyone even takes the module seriously and many tutorials and their TAs do not even enforce this. There was also a supposed debate week, but it ended up being more similar to what the weekly group discussion was like. Lastly, the group project which involved creating a product and discussing the ethics of it ended up as just a simple presentation where everyone just reads off their phonnes. Grading was so variable and subjective that I honestly did not care about it. Finals was an open book MCQ paper that had pretty irrelevant content to be completely honest with you. Also, they clearly cannot plan things right if you have 3 separate venues and still have people sitting on the floor of a lecture theatre to do their Final exam. The whole module seemed more of a formality than anything else. You tell people that you took a module on ethics and they go, 'oh cool'. But in reality, it was just a waste of time.
closingRemarks: Try your luck in finals. If you score well, good. If not, S/U.

name: CFG1002: Career Catalyst
intro: Module that lasts half a semester and aims to help students with their career in the forseeable future.
review: Very low workload module that essentially involves a few e-learning lessons and a workshop that teaches you about navigating towards career readiness. By the end of the module, you would have the chance to create a resume as well as try out a mock interview using the VMOCK platform. There are a few quizzes here and there which are very simple to score in and should not be an issue.
closingRemarks: Mostly forgettable module but it does help you create a resume if you already do not have one.

name: CFG1004: Financial Wellbeing - Art and Science of Investing
intro: Module that does not tell you what to invest, but what to look out for should you wish to invest.
review: Nothing much to cover here too. This module is a follow-up to the financial management module CFG1002, and instead teaches you about how one can grow your wealth through investing. It has the same structure of OTOT e-learning lessons and goes through the basics of investing, the different types of investments, the risks and rewards of each and how to manage your portfolio.
closingRemarks: Chill 2 MC module that could potentially help people who wish to get into inevsting. Commonly taken by people who have no idea what to do with their free MCs.

name: CS2101: Effective Communication for Computing Professionals
intro: The second of the 2 dreaded 'presentation' modules that all CS students have to face. Has to be taken alongside CS2103T.
review: Relatively notorious module that most people save their S/U credits for as well. I was not looking forward to it, but looking back I guess I did luck out in several aspects and the experience turned out to not be too bad. As expected from a communications module, the assessment basically involved presentation after presentation after presentation. In the first session of week 1, we were informed that there will be approximately 7 to 8 presentation, inclusive of rehearsals for the actual CA graded ones. That was enough to make me want to sack off the module, but the one saving grace was that I took the module with 4 other people I knew and the in the small class of 20, I lucked out when I was grouped with 2 of them for our first presentation. This was relatively simple and involed sharing insights into a particular article that we were to read up on and present to the class. The first CA (2nd presentation) involved the same group of 3 and this time required a longer presentation including content slides on a chosen communication topic (My group was assigned Emotional Intelligence). The first half of the module had tutorials basically alternating between some a speedrun of some content regarding communication skills, rehearsals for presentations and then the actual presentations themselves. In the second half, we had 3 CAs, thankfully only 1 of them involved a presentation. This presentation, however, was done in parallel with the software development project in CS2103T. In a way, this helped in preparation of the content for this presentation, since we were now sharing about a product we were actively working on instead of a random topic under the sun. It involved establishing a proper setting for the presentation such as a Tech Convention or a Shareholders meeting and having to adhere to such settings, be it dressing the part (formal wear) and ensuring that a non-technical audience is still able to understand the presentation. I was fortunate enough to have a group that I already knew, so navigating through both the development aspect in CS2103T and the presentation aspect in CS2101 was not too difficult. For CA3, it basically was just a submission of a written User Guide on the application developed in CS2103T that likewise adheres to the target audience the product is meant for. The final CA was an interesting one and is something that my personal TA and the course coordinator were working on. 'Insightful Musings' was an unessay assignment where you could submit your reflections of the module in any form you wish. the only catch is that it cannot be an essay. I initially was very excited to create a board game that depicts my journey through the module but after some discussion with my TA, it ended up falling through since there wouldn't be a proper way to evaluate and grade it objectively. Ideas of some form of artpiece also fell through. In the end, I went with a more vanilla option in a 'Draw my Life' video which I rushed out in a day or 2. Not too confident in my drawing skills, let alone my narration ability but it will have to do. Many people do not enjoy this module and I can definitely relate to them. The sheer amount of presentations is way too much especially for someone like me who absolutely despises public speaking. Content wise, it also involved a lot of fluffy content which frankly, will probably not be used in actual real life situations too. Setting those aside, I still did have a somewhat pleasant experience, mainly due to the class and tutor I had. The class was surprisingly funny to hang out with and really gave me nostalgia of highschool and JC vibes. It was nice to see so many people in class, including the TA share the same interest in games, allowing for some fun conversations before class stated and even during some breaks. I have seen NUSmod reviews complaining of subjective grading due to bias and I can definitely understand their point of view, but the game is the game I guess; The one time playing so many degenerate games helped in my academic life.
closingRemarks: An introvert's worst nightmare. Do take with as many friends as you can. Do have a positive mindset though and you will benefit. Despite the fluff and workload, I did actually see significant progress and improvement in my presentation ability.

name: CS2103T + CS2103R: Software Engineering
intro: Honestly, one of the modules I enjoyed taking the most as of yet, so much so I even did an extension of it as a summer project (CS2103R).
review: The moment I saw that the module had a good looking and organized website dedicated for it, one that also makes use of various other projects (RepoSense, TeamMates etc.) the Professor led to build, I knew this module would definitely be up there in terms of how it is conducted. Really appreciated how basically everything you wish to know related to the module was essentially already available from the very start, be it how a typical week would look like, what the grade breakdown is and even what tools we will be using and how to install them. Personally, I took advantage of this and read up early on some of the earlier topics given that the first week was a refresher on Java and OOP concepts, allowing me to have a small headstart on learning Git using the Git learning trail they also provided us with. With this, I was personally very comfortable easing in into this module and able to start working on the iP straightaway while some others were beginning to start wrestling with the sudden influx of information not only from this module, but from their other modules too. Not sure if that makes sense, but TLDR, it allowed me to be prepared for everything to do with the module and not be overwhelmed with any admin information. The one unique thing about this module would be the consistent coursework, which I personally have not encountered in any of the other modules I have taken, in the sense that we had 2 main projects, an brownfield and a greenfield one, spanning each semester half. These projects were to be done incremently, with the weekly additions being based on the content covered that same week. This felt like a really efficient way to reinforce the concepts taught as we were able to apply them almost immediately after learning them. The iP project is a rather simple project that was only as complex as you made it out to be. Its main aim, I would say, was to prepare us for the subsequent tP, by having us put into practise Git as well as SWE practises like documentation, all while getting used to JAVA OOP coding once again. We essentially had several milestones to hit each week, starting from a simple CLI chatbot and evolving it into our own personalised assistant chatbot with its own customized GUI. I really enjoyed this first half and probably way spent more time on it than I myself would expect. It was surprisingly fun having the freedom to do whatever I want despite the academic setting and I was also learning new things in the process. In the second half, we were tasked to take over a brownfield project AB3, and modify it into our own personal product. My group decided on some form of hiring manager application wehich allows for streamlined onboarding of new employees. Sounds really grand and hard to achieve, but too be far I am pretty sure all the other groups also had similar ideas. At the end of the day, they were restrictions put in place to limit the workload we would create for ourselves so every group likely had their plans reduced to similar basic CRUD applications, just reskinned to fit whatever concept their group came up with. With that said, it didn't mean that there was nothing to learn though. In fact, this project was a lot more complex than the iP, with the need to understand the existing codebase, the need to refactor and add new features, and the need to work with a team to ensure that everything is done properly. And while doing so, we also had to make sure all the proper documentation was done and prepare for the CA presentation to be done in CS2101. Workload definitely seemed heavier, but honestly with a group that I am already comfortable with and proper delegation, it wasn't too bad. The next highlight would be the Practical Assessment, which once I again was a new experience for me. In this module, the PA was a timed bug catching period where each person is assigned another group's product and tasked to test them thoroughly, with the grading being based on the number and severity of bugs found. I was honestly pretty scared of this component at first but when I got down to it, it was actually pretty enjoyable. Afterwards, we got together as a team and had to respond to the bugs found in our own product and basically engage with the testers to justify whether their critique was valid or simply accept our oversight on certain issues. Last component would be the Finals, which honestly is not too much different from other modules. Rather manageable paper that had its fair share of simple and tricky questions. The whole experience felt a lot more like an entertaining workshop than a typical school module and I definitely enjoyed it. Teaching staff were honestly really good, with everyone being very quick to respond to queries and very helpful in guiding us through the content (Forum was definitely a goldmine albeit some pariticipation point farmers). Tutorial with the other Prof leading the module Ganesh was also really chill and useful. With all the lecture content being available on the website, I didn't really watch the lectures; I only tune in for information on administative issues or updates and announcements. There is still room for improvement for the module though even though I am the biggest glazer of it. The low hanging fruit would definitely be the grading system of the PA, with many complaints of it being zero-sum, where points you gain from identifying a bug is deducted from the person responsible for the bug. This also led to people being desperate and simply prioritizing quantity over quality and swarming groups with excessive bug reports, most of which are absolute garbage and no-effort gibberish. This results in so much time and effort wasted as well as a layer of anxiety and stress amongst students that definitely is not appreciated. Exacerbating this problem would be how the groups are formed. Yes there is freedom in forming your own groups but they have to fulfill certain diversity requirements (Bless my diverse friend group of 2 even though I am the most basic a CS person can be). Many students, particularly the international students and the rare occurring female race (🤓☝️), were forced into joining existing friend groups and potentially will not have a good time in that dynamic. I have seen/heard incidents of workload unfairness and it sucks to know that this could be prevented simply by lifting the diversity restriction. Not sure if this on the 01 or the 03 side, but it really should not be in place; even with the criteria, every group ends up being predominantly basic Singaporean Chinese Male anyway. Still, I do respect the teaching staff, especially Prof Damith for coordinating this module and am proud to say that this is the first CS module I thoroughly enjoyed.
closingRemarks: To close, I just wish to touch on CS2103R which I did as a Summer extension project to the module. It definitely ended up requiring more effort than I expected for a 1 mc module but it was a unique experience anyway. I basically was assigned a few tasks by Prof Damith himself to help out with upgrading the projects we worked on in CS2103T to a later version of Java. Subsequently, he gave us free reign to explore the various OSS projects he is a part of and contribute to them. I ended up adding a very simple guide on how to install and configure Java on Windows on the se-education page, tinkering with MarkBind in the process. I also had the opportunity to write up a proposal on how to improve the CS2103T module where I suggested the idea of introducing SemVer and evaluated the pros and cons oo it. It was a really unique experience and I am glad I took up the opportunity to work with Prof Damith for a little longer.

name: CS2106: Introduction to Operating Systems
intro: Another core module that builds on CS2100 and covers everything to do with Operating Systems.
review: Touted as a relatively difficult module with a lot content to memorise. I can confirm that that is indeed true. The module covers the basics of Operating Systems, starting with a brief history and its structure and architecture. It then moves on to 3 main topics, Process, Memory and File Management. The first half kicks off with our old friend MIPS to better illustrate how processes work. I really was not happy seeing its return but thankfully it lasted just the first tutorial. Subsequently, everything was basically new knowledge. I do not wish to go in depth to the content covered btu I will try to provide a brief summary. The first big topic was on processes: which is basically an instance of a program. We covered everything to do with process: what consitutes one, their different states, the different functions to create and navigate between these states, and the different scheduling algorithms that can be used to manage them. We also learnt about how such process interact and communicate with one another, and also the issue of synchronization, which is definitely the most complex and mind boggling aspect of the processes topic and arguably the whole module. Till now, I can't say I am confident in implementing a sempahore or mutex to solve Dining Philosopher's or similar synchronization problems. Next up, we have memoery management which honestly seemed more intuitive to learn. It started out with assumptions of how memory is managed in the OS. As we moved on to cover aspects like paging and segmentation, these assumptions were lifted to illustrate the problems that such methods were addressing. Admittedly, it can get really confusing especially when trying to figure out the different page tables and trying to translate them but with enough effort and practise, it can be done (or so I heard, I was and still am really bad at it). Last up was File management which I would say is the easiest of the 3, since we have the most experience with it, given that any one that uses a computer would have interacted with a file or 2 (million). Lectures were not too bad, but because of the sheer volume of content, it was hard to keep up with live pace and I preferred watching recordings later on. Watching earlier recordings from 2019 also helped quite a bit. Tutorials were conducted weekly and I had a pretty good tutor, so it had a relatively fine experience there too. As for the 4 labs, it ended up as pair work through a list of tasks before turning up for your lab session to present a code demonstration to a TA and answer some questions if the need arises. The labs were not too difficult but having to refresh on C and learn a bit of scripting did take some time and effort (Once again, ChatGPT and Google are great here). Midterms was an all MCQ paper but consisted of some pretty tricky questions that I definitely fell for. On the bright side, there were some ambiguous questions that resulted in the midterm constantly being regraded for quite a while. Finals still had some MCQs but also involved open ended questions that required more brain work. I honestly cannot recall too much about it, meaning that it was probably an average paper, not too easy but also not difficult to the point where I get PTSD from it. Ultimately, decent module once again, content heavy but manageable with consistent work and effort. Teaching staff is also fairly comptetent. Prof Nitya the admin goat.
closingRemarks: You cannot escape this unless you fly to another country. Just try your best to keep up with the content and you should be fine.

name: IS2218: DIgital Platforms for Business
intro: Relatively new module that covers the basics of digital platforms and how they can be used in a business setting.
review: The module starts off with some accounting basics and financial statement analysis in the first half. It then moves on to the time value of money and introduces platform thinking, and finally ending with marketing. Really low workload, consisting of 4 homework assignments, one of which is a fully paid for Coursera module. The other 3 are relatively simple calculation questions that should not take more than a day to complete. Both the Midterm and Finals were short 20 MCQ papers which were relatively straight forward as well. Midterm only covers the first half and Finals covers the second half so it was much easier to prepare for both assessments too. There were not many PYPs since it is a new module after all but the teaching team did provide a few example questions to refer to. Content was honestly somewhat interesting but it was let down by the cohort that honestly outdid the typical CS cohort I deal with in terms of immaturity and lack of respect. The Professor definitely has the knowledge and is very willing to engage the class during his lectures but it reakky is a shame that the class did not reciprocate. Watching it through the live session was also extremely cringe inducing, seeing people in the LIVE physical venue just straight up conversing with one another over the professor's lecture. It also did not help that the professor did not really try to control them and even acknowledged some of the evidently 'troll' questions that were raised in the PollEV. I would say that the content was interesting and the workload was low, but the cohort really made the experience a lot worse than it should have been.
closingRemarks: Pretty low workload, low brainpower module that is mildly interesting. Perfect for clearing a Interdisciplinary requirement if you can deal with immature idiots. Or just don't watch the lectures

name: ST2334: Probability and Statistics
intro: Finally ther last of the 3 foundational math modules that CS students have to take. Name explains it all.
review: Really nothing much to it. Just a bunch of probability and statistics content that you have to understand, some of which was covered in JC, some not. This isn't the module you are looking for if you really want to learn about propoer statistics since this covers more basic content, so if you do have this as a core module, that's good. Content wise, it isn't too difficult to understand, but do note that some questions can get pretty tricky especially if you are not careful with your calculations. Lectures were kind of redundant since the pre lecture videos can basially function as the lecture themselves and there was already a detailed set of notes to be referred to provided at the very start of the module. Tutorials were somewhat manageable and actually useful since they usually featured questions that were similar to those from PYPs. Revising these questions would definitely benefit when preparing for assessments. Midterm was on the easier side and was not too much of an issue (I was really careless though). Finals was where the difficulty suddenly spiked but at that point, I really lost all care for the module and was focusing more on other modules.
closingRemarks: Just cram the week before the assessments and you should be fine. Bell curve is steep so you should't expect much anyway.

name: ALS1010: Learning to Learn Better
intro: Somewhat fluff 2 mc module that really doesn't mean much
review: Really nothing much to say about this module. It is a 2 MC module where you just turn up for online lecture attendance. The content is somewhat basic and personally I feel does not really benefit you much. Sure, it does teach you some study techniques and how to manage your time better, but I feel that most of these are things that you would already know, have heard of or have been actively practising without knowing and just off intuition. The part I enjoyed the most was unironically the guest lecture that most people disliked: The topic covering Sleep. I was mildly intrigued by the facts presented by the guest lecturer and in fact was not put to sleep by it, unliike most of my peers. The assignments were simply just filling out a template on your goals and how you wish to achieve them.
closingRemarks: If you need a 2 mc module, this is a very forgettable low workload module that you can consider.

name: GEC1044: Chinese Medicine: Theory and Practice
intro: A module I took simply because the content seemed intersting and I wanted to learn more about it for trivia knowledge purposes.
review: Really liked the Prof's manner of presenting the module content in his lectures. It really felt like I was watching a well-edited documentary rather than an academic lecture. That lasted for only the first semester half unfortunately, as he managed to bring in a guest lecturer per week for the second half to share their respective expertise regarding Chinese Medicine. The content was really interesting and I did learn a lot about the different aspects of Chinese Medicine, from the history of it, to the different types of treatments and the different philosophies that underpin it. The tutorials felt a bit more of a chore to attend but was bearable as there wasn't much effort involved throughout. The online forum near the end of the semester was also kind of a hassle since I had to do it during my commute to school due to its timing but it was not too difficult to complete. Highlight was definitely the field trip to Thong Chai Medical Institute, where we had a fun workshop and even got to experience acupunture and cupping. Regrettably, I was not in the best of health that day and ended up feeling really lightheaded during the session. As for the report, it was really straightforward. The individual assignment on the other hand, took a little more time than I wished to complete it but rather than being difficult, it felt more frustrating having to research and describe the different types of ingredients I chose to use in my herbal recipe. If you are willing to tough it out through the essay assignment, the rest of the moduel, in my opinion, is worth taking.
closingRemarks: Surprisingly enjoyable module both content wise and workload wise. The content was interesting and the workload was manageable. The field trip was also a nice touch.

name: HSI2013: The Science of Music
intro: A module that I bidded for on a whim and ended up really enjoying.
review: Bidded for this in the last round with only 1 available slot left and over a hundred other bidders. Somehow got the module and felt like my decision to attend the Genshin concert was justified. The module content however honestly was not the most interesting and that is not due to the 10 year old lecture videos we were given, but it truly was just the content that did not appeal to me as much. The pace at which the content was taught is excruciatingly slow, but understandable as people without a music or science background may be taking the module, until you realise that quite a significant amount definitely do music composition in their free time. Nonetheless, the fact that I was able to use on Genshin Concert experience as an academic essay was enough to carry me through the module. Other than the essay, there was a MIDI music composition that I honestly did not put much effort into. It really felt kind of hopeless trying to score in thsi category without any prior knowledge in it and after seeing other students who were already well versed in it. The Midterm and Finals were both open book MCQ papers that were relatively simple to score in especially if you managed to get your hands on PYPs which had the exact same question format for the most part. Still carelessness was an issue, as a wrong calculation adandn the paper's weird tendency to favour 'None of the above' options could do you in. Still, relatively low workload module that can be overloaded with.
closingRemarks: Took it to justify spending money on a concert. No regrets at all.

name: LAJ1201: Japanese 1
intro: Pretty high workload module in terms of committment and effort to grade ratio.
review: Essentially the best way to kickstart actually learning Japanese especially if you do not have the discipline to study it on your own. This module really really rewards consistent effort. It does not matter how much work you put into the module if it is not done in regular intervals; There is no point to cramming all the vocabulary or grammar rules the day before a test (not like that is possible anyway), just to forget it right after the examination. Not only does it not work most of the time, it also defeats the very purpose of learning a new language. This isn't like other technical modules you may find in your majors where even if you miss out on understanding some content, you can eventually catch up or you simply regard it as giving up that small bit of knowledge. It really is very unforgiving to miss any form of content here given it really covers the absolute most basic and most foundational aspects critical for learning Japanese. The moment you falter, the accumulated backlog and effort required to get back on track is honestly not worth and is probably why some people end up giving up and simply S/U-ing it or straight up dropping the module midway. The way the grade breakdown is like also makes it such that if you really do care about the grade, you have to be consistent in doing all the different homework tasks, be it penmanship, voice reording or the homework sheets. Not only that, you also have to prepare for weekly vocab quizzes during tutorials and also try your best to actively participate in the actual class. All these small tasks, on top of the test components (Listening Comprehension Quizzes, Oral Interviews and Term Tests), all contribute to your final grade. Essentially, every little thing counts and the best way to guarantee a good learning experience and a good grade would be to put in effort in everything. The main hurdle I personally struggled with would be the earlier weeks where you have limited time (kind of) to get used to and ideally memorise the 2 alphabets systems, Hiragana and Katakana. The module is already very forgiving in the sense that they do teach as much of it in English as possible, but without a decent grasp of the basic building blocks of the language, it will make life impossibly difficult for the subsequent weeks. Overall, I did enjoy the module quite a lot as I finally was able to put to use 10 years of Japanese culture knowledge into actual language learning. I took the module alone and I took that as a way to force myself out of my comfort zone and engage more during class disussions, which turned out relatively well. It also helped that the tutors were all extremely friendly and the structure of the tutorials essentially forces everyone to speak up in class and learn from one another. once again, it reminds me of highschool and JC days, where you have constant interaction with the same group of people and actively making, learning and helping one another along the way. I really do not have much issues with the module. Sure content is rather heavy, but what else can you expect from a language module. I admit a 6 hour committment weekly is really high, but in hindsight it is the amount of practice these long hours gave us that allows us to be able to have such a module in the first place. Picking up a new language in 13 weeks is lowkey crazy to begin with. Smurfing is definitely an potential issue but I feel that it is more of a personal issue than a module issue. I do not think the module can do much to prevent smurfing, especially when the smurfer wishes to avoid detection. It is really up to the individual to decide if they just want a free A grade or if they really wish to learn the language at a higher level. Personally, I would not consider myself a smurf compared to some peers I have seen, but I do admit I certainly have an advantage over many others who have not been exposed to Japanese before. But, that is also because I actively immerse myself in the culture. My Spotify is literally exclusively Jpop and Jrock, I watch Japanese anime, read Japanese manga, play (vicariously sometimes) Japanese games and I watch lots of Japanese stream content. But even then, I still had to put in substantial effort to learn Hiragana, Katakana and all the grammartical rules. An advantage I have are possibly in the vocab department since I some of them were familiar to me, though I still had to learn how to write them. another advantage would probably be in the oral department, listening and especially speaking came more naturally for me and pronunciation and intonation is much easier for me to pick up. But even then, there were still many things I had to learn and I still had to put in the effort to learn them. I do admit smurfs are a problem but after taking the module, I think they do not have as much of an advantage as I thought they had before. Of course, this is referring to people that are on the lower end. People who have qualifications like JLPT N2 and are still taking the module are a different story, but those I find are quite rare. I am more referring to people who maybe studied certain parts of the language already e.g. already learnt the alphabet system or have taken a similar module outside before. Honestly, after thinking and yapping so much about the module, maybe smurfs aren't really a problem. The actual fluent ones probably will not be taking this module anyway. The ones that are not so fluent but may have some prior knowledge still have to put in decent effort to fit into the system and consistently perform well. In that sense, maybe the module is fine as it is. My head is a mess man. TLDR: Really fun module. Put in effort and you will be rewarded.
closingRemarks: Just to get it off my chest and no I swear I'm not coping, the EdX module on conversational Japanese I took as a DYOC module before did not help in ANY way. That module literally focused on common phrases used in the context of an international student in Japan and did not cover any basic grammar or vocab. It didn't even cover Hiragana and Katakana. It felt more like I was preparing to go for a holiday and I googled 'Useful phrases to know when visiting Japan'.  If anything, getting back into anime benefited a lot more.

name: CS3230: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
intro: This module needs no introduction.
review: Don't know how to begin this review and honestly that is the same thought I had attempting any of the questions in this module. I knew it was going to be tough but it really had me by the balls and not in a good way. I ended up taking this alone, not according to plan due to some circumstances, and honestly felt great initally knowing that Prof Steven Halim was taking it instead of Prof Arnab. I thought having better administrative competence would help ease some of the pain I would get from the content but it didn't. First 2 weeks were still manageable, covering some familiar concepts just with more depth: Orders of Growth, Reccurence Relations and Master Theorem. It was not too difficult to understand. the only issue I had was probably the problems involving some sort of proving but that was to be expected. I just cannot do proving questions. Nothing more to it. Unfortunately for me, this was the part of the module where having a good foundation in writing proofs becomes valuable. Starting from the lecture on 'Proof of Correctness', it was only downhill from there. I did somewhat understand the concepts behind topics like DnC, Dynamic Programmming and Greedy Algorithms but attempting the questions without any help seemed to disprove that fact. Only thing not random regarding Randomized Algorithm problems is the fact that i have a 100% chance of not being able to solve it. Amortized surprisingly slowly grew on me but I am not sure if that was because I felt confident in my attempt on the AA question in Finals (which I didn't even get full credit for, but thats better than 0), but that was enough to have me prefer it over the rest. Problem reductions and Np completeness honestly seemed like a really interesting topic to explore at your own pace. I repeat at your own pace. Having to stress over the need to prove all the already proven problem statements was not my cup of tea (I can't even take caffeine lol).
